beats.intro: Chapter one, lesson two. Structural classification: the side chains. [[bricks]]Picture a box of building bricks. Every brick has the same base, the same studs underneath, so they all snap together. But on top, each brick carries a different shape. [[top]]An amino acid is just like that. Every one has the same backbone: the amino group, the carboxyl group, the alpha carbon and a hydrogen. What makes it different is the side chain, called R. [[card]]Here is our amino acid card from lesson one. Today we light the first tab, Structural: sorting amino acids by the shape of R. [[four]]The slide sorts them into four families: aliphatic, aromatic, heterocyclic and imino.
beats.families: [[open]]The big question is simply this. Is the side chain an open chain, or does it contain a ring? [[ali]]Aliphatic means an open chain, with no ring. It is the largest family, and it has six subgroups. [[aro]]Aromatic means a benzene ring. [[het]]Heterocyclic means a ring that holds an atom other than carbon, here nitrogen. [[imi]]And imino is the odd one out: a ring in which the nitrogen of the amino group itself is part of the ring. Keep that picture in mind. We come back to it at the end.
beats.simple: [[gly]]Start with aliphatic, subgroup a: the simple ones. Glycine has R equal to a single hydrogen. It is the smallest side chain there is. [[ala]]Alanine adds one carbon: R is a methyl group, C H three. [[ser]]Subgroup b: hydroxy-containing. Serine is alanine with an O H group on the end of its side chain. [[thr]]Threonine has an O H group too, on a side chain of two carbons. Hydroxy simply means O H, the same group you find in an alcohol.
beats.sulfur: [[cys]]Subgroup c: sulfur-containing. Cysteine carries an S H group, called a sulfhydryl group: a sulfur with a hydrogen on it. [[met]]Methionine also has sulfur, but tucked inside the chain, with a methyl group on the end and no hydrogen. [[pair]]Now cystine, spelled with an I N E. It is not one amino acid with its own side chain. [[ss]]Take two cysteines. Each loses the hydrogen from its S H group, and the two sulfurs join in a single bond: a disulfide bridge. Two cysteines joined by a disulfide bridge make cystine. [[note]]The slide lists it in this group, so we do too. You will meet the disulfide bridge again, holding proteins in shape.
beats.q1: Quick check. What is cystine made of?
beats.branched: [[val]]Subgroup d: branched-chain. Valine, leucine and isoleucine. Look for the fork in the side chain. Valine is a C H carrying two methyl groups, like a small letter Y. [[leu]]Leucine puts one extra C H two between the alpha carbon and the fork. [[ile]]Isoleucine has the same atoms as leucine, but arranged differently: the branch point sits right next to the alpha carbon, with a methyl group on it and a short tail behind. [[three]]Three amino acids, one subgroup: each a branch of carbon and hydrogen only.
beats.charged: [[asp]]Subgroups e and f carry a charge. Acidic: aspartic acid and glutamic acid. Each has a second carboxyl group in R. Aspartic acid has a short arm. [[glu]]Glutamic acid has an arm one carbon longer. [[arg]]Basic: arginine, a long chain that ends in a group with several nitrogens, and lysine, a chain of four carbons that ends in an amino group. [[six]]Count the subgroups again. Simple, hydroxy, sulfur, branched, acidic and basic. Six, from a to f.
beats.q2: Quick check. A side chain ends in a second carboxyl group. Is it acidic or basic?
beats.rings: [[benz]]Now the rings. Aromatic means a benzene ring: six carbons in a hexagon, with alternating double bonds. Phenylalanine is a benzene ring on a C H two arm. [[tyr]]Tyrosine is the same, plus an O H group on the far side of the ring. A benzene ring carrying an O H is called a phenol group. [[indole]]Heterocyclic. Tryptophan has an indole ring: a benzene ring joined to a five-sided ring that holds one nitrogen with its hydrogen. Two rings sharing one edge. [[imid]]Histidine has an {{imidazole|im-id-AZ-ole}} ring: five-sided, with two nitrogens. [[note]]Some books put tryptophan under aromatic, because it contains a benzene ring, and histidine is also basic. We follow the lecture: both are heterocyclic. [[pro]]Last, proline. Its ring is five-sided with one nitrogen: a {{pyrrolidine|pir-ROL-ih-deen}} ring. That nitrogen is the amino group itself, bent round to join the side chain. That is why proline is called an imino acid.
beats.sort: Let's sort a few, with two questions. First: is there a ring? Second: if so, what is in it? [[s1]]A side chain that is just one hydrogen. No ring, simple: glycine. [[s2]]An open chain ending in a second carboxyl group. No ring, acidic. [[s3]]A hexagon of carbons. A ring with only carbon: aromatic. [[s4]]A five-sided ring with two nitrogens. Heterocyclic: histidine. [[s5]]A five-sided ring that includes the amino nitrogen. Imino: proline.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Structural classification sorts amino acids by the side chain, R. [[s2]]No ring means aliphatic, with six subgroups: simple, hydroxy, sulfur, branched, acidic and basic. [[s3]]A benzene ring: aromatic, phenylalanine and tyrosine. A ring with a nitrogen: heterocyclic, tryptophan and histidine. And proline, with the amino nitrogen in the ring: imino. [[s4]]One last note. The slide lists nineteen names. Asparagine and glutamine, two more of the twenty, are not on it, and cystine is not one of the twenty at all, because it is two cysteines joined. [[end]]Now try the practice.
